candidate.blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — medication administration, adverse effects, interactions and monitoring
candidate.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — anticoagulant monitoring
candidate.educational_objective: Distinguish appropriate enoxaparin safety monitoring from routine aPTT-based titration used with unfractionated heparin.

options.A: Routine aPTT testing is used to titrate every enoxaparin dose.
options.B: PT/INR is the preferred routine test for adjusting enoxaparin therapy.
options.C: PT and aPTT are not adequate for monitoring its anticoagulant effect; anti-factor Xa levels may be used in selected situations.
options.D: No laboratory or clinical monitoring is needed while the client receives enoxaparin.

candidate.rationale: The current enoxaparin label states that PT and aPTT are not adequate for monitoring enoxaparin's anticoagulant effect. Safety monitoring includes CBC/platelets and assessment for bleeding. Anti-factor Xa levels may be used in selected circumstances, including renal impairment or when abnormal coagulation parameters or bleeding occur. Therefore C is correct.
candidate.source_claim_supported: PT and aPTT are not adequate for monitoring enoxaparin anticoagulant effects; anti-factor Xa may be used in selected clinical circumstances; CBC/platelets and bleeding surveillance are part of safety monitoring.
candidate.source_organization: DailyMed / U.S. National Library of Medicine
candidate.stem: A client is receiving subcutaneous enoxaparin. Which statement about laboratory monitoring is most accurate?
